title: Chorea-acanthocytosis: a case report
case_prompt:
A 36-year-old right-handed woman presented with gradually worsening abnormal facial movements over several years, characterized by intermittent rapid forceful eye closure, perioral movements, and lower-lip biting. Her husband noted progressive difficulty speaking and swallowing and weakness of all four limbs; she was wheelchair-bound. There was no family history of neurologic disease, and she had no exposure to medications known to cause extrapyramidal dysfunction.

On examination, she had orofaciolingual dyskinesias mimicking suckling and grimacing and a lower-lip ulcer from repeated biting. Formal cognitive testing could not be performed due to unintelligible speech. There was wasting of all four limbs, muscle strength of 4/5, and diminished deep tendon reflexes. Funduscopy and sensory examination were normal; there was no Kayser–Fleischer ring, cerebellar signs, or autonomic dysfunction.

Laboratory studies revealed a serum creatine kinase level of 528 U/L (normal ≤165 U/L). A peripheral blood smear demonstrated acanthocytes. Nerve conduction studies showed a peripheral mixed axonal neuropathy. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed degenerative changes in the basal ganglia. Routine blood counts, liver and renal function tests, glucose, autoimmune serologies, serum copper and ceruloplasmin levels, viral serologies (HIV, hepatitis B and C), cerebrospinal fluid analysis, abdominal ultrasonography, electrocardiography, and echocardiography were all within normal limits.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Drug-induced movement disorder — “She was not exposed to long-term medications known to cause extrapyramidal dysfunction.”  
2. Wilson’s disease — “Kayser–Fleischer ring... and serum ceruloplasmin... were normal.”  
3. HDL2 and pantothenate kinase–associated neurodegeneration — “HDL2 and pantothenate kinase–associated neurodegeneration have a childhood or juvenile onset, and HDL2 is usually found in patients with African ancestry.”  
4. McLeod syndrome — “MLS is an X-linked disorder that has predominant cardiovascular manifestations... Also, lip biting is exceedingly rare in MLS... female sex in our case rules out MLS.”  
5. Chorea-acanthocytosis — “ChAc consists of choreoathetoid movement disorder with orofacial dyskinesia... involuntary tongue- and lip-biting.”
